Swapping is a memory management technique used in operating systems to manage the allocation of memory resources. It involves moving data between main memory (RAM) and secondary storage (like a hard disk drive or SSD) to optimize the use of available memory. When a process needs more memory than is available in RAM, the operating system can temporarily move some of the process's data from RAM to secondary storage (a process called swapping out), freeing up RAM for other processes. Later, when that process needs to access the swapped-out data again, the operating system will move it back into RAM (swapping in). This allows the system to run more processes than can fit in RAM at once, effectively extending the available memory capacity.             try:

You can use a hyperlink or use a VBA macro to open a webpage automatically during your presentation.
For hyperlink:
1. Select the text or object you want to turn into a link.
2. Go to the Insert tab, click on Hyperlink.
3. Choose "Existing File or Web Page".
4. Enter the URL of the webpage you want to open.
5. Click "Add".
6. When you click on the link during your presentation, it will open the webpage in a new tab.
For VBA macro:
1. Press Alt + F11 to open the Visual Basic Editor.
2. Go to Insert > Module.
3. Paste the following code:
function OpenWebpage (URL) {
Shell ( "C:\Program Files\Internet Explorer iexplore.exe" & URL)
}
4. Save the presentation as a macro-enabled file (.pptm).
5. Assign the macro to a slide or a button.
6. When you run the macro during your presentation, it will open the webpage in Internet Explorer.

Zero-knowledge proofs are a type of cryptographic protocol that allows one party to prove to another party that a statement is true without revealing any information about the statement itself. This means that the prover can convince the verifier that they know something without giving away any of the details. This is a very important concept in cryptography, as it allows for secure communication and verification of information without exposing sensitive data.

In a zero-knowledge proof, the prover and verifier are two parties that are trying to verify a statement. The prover wants to convince the verifier that a certain statement is true, but they do not want to reveal any information about the statement itself. The verifier, on the other hand, wants to be sure that the statement is true without learning any additional information.

To understand how zero-knowledge proofs work, it is helpful to think about a real-world example. Let's say that a person wants to prove that they know the password to a secure system. Without revealing the password itself, they want to convince the system that they know it. This is where zero-knowledge proofs come in. The person could use a zero-knowledge proof to demonstrate that they know the password without giving it away.

Another example is in the field of blockchain technology. In a blockchain, transactions are verified by a network of nodes.             sample\_probs = F.softmax(sample\_logits, dim=-1)
